name: Data centre grid interaction (demand response and frequency services)
aliases: Data centre demand response and flexible load
applications: frequency containment and dynamic containment schemes
principle: The data centre's own UPS fleet doubles as a grid asset: when frequency dips below nominal, inverters draw from batteries instead of the grid for seconds to minutes — no IT impact — and the operator sells that as frequency response. Enel X's Digital Realty deployment in Ireland responds in under half a second; Microsoft is rolling out UPS battery-sharing worldwide and pushed for the UK's Dynamic Containment scheme to open to data centres after Ireland led; UK NESO programmes now listed for data centres include Demand Flexibility Service, Dynamic Containment, Dynamic Moderation, Dynamic Regulation and Static FFR. Battery-cycling degradation is the principal trade-off.

advantages: Turns existing backup batteries into a revenue stream
No IT downtime — the load rides on batteries while the grid sees less demand
limitations: Battery wear from cycling — VRLA fleets degrade faster than lithium
Market access varies by jurisdiction (Ireland open, UK opening)
Operators must protect the backup mission margin first
